REL13-BP02 Use defined recovery strategies to meet the recovery objectives
A workload needs a planned way to run from a recovery site when its
    primary location cannot serve it. Choosing that plan is a trade-off
    between how fast you recover and how much standing infrastructure
    you pay for and operate. Define a strategy for each workload, drawn
    from a small set of reusable patterns.
Desired outcome:
Each workload has a defined, implemented disaster recovery
        strategy that meets its recovery objectives.
Workloads with similar objectives reuse the same recovery
        patterns and tooling.
Your strategy accounts for both service failover and the
        protection of data against corruption.
You have a documented plan for returning operation to the
        primary site after an event.
Common anti-patterns:
Teams implement inconsistent recovery procedures for workloads
        that share the same objectives.
Recovery is left to be improvised when a disaster occurs, with
        no strategy defined in advance.
A workload has no disaster recovery plan at all.
Recovery depends on control plane operations that may be
        unavailable during the event.
Benefits of establishing this best
    practice:
Common tooling and test procedures become possible because
        recovery follows defined patterns.
Teams share knowledge and implement recovery more consistently
        across the workloads they own.
Recovery objectives are more likely to be met because the
        strategy is planned, implemented, and tested.
Level of risk exposed if this best practice
    is not established:
High. Without a planned, implemented,
    and tested strategy, you are unlikely to meet recovery objectives
    during a disaster.
Implementation guidance
The recovery site can be a separate set of Availability Zones
      within one AWS Region or a separate Region. Multiple Availability
      Zones protect against localized events such as fires, floods, and
      power loss. A separate Region protects against the rare event that
      makes an entire Region unavailable, though regulatory
      data-residency rules sometimes rule this out.
The following figure lists the four strategies in increasing order
      of cost and decreasing order of RTO and RPO.
Backup and restore
copies data and
          applications to the recovery site and rebuilds on demand,
          giving an RPO in hours and an RTO of up to a day.
Pilot light
keeps core data replicated
          and always on while compute stays dormant until needed,
          reaching an RPO in minutes and an RTO in tens of minutes.
Warm standby
runs a scaled-down but fully
          functional copy that you scale up on failover, reaching an RPO
          in seconds and an RTO in minutes.
Multi-site active-active
serves live
          traffic from more than one Region, pushing RPO and RTO toward
          zero at the highest operational cost.
Disaster recovery strategies from backup and restore to multi-site active-active
Pilot light and warm standby both keep a copy of primary-site
      assets in the recovery site with data replicated and live. The
      difference is readiness. A pilot light cannot serve requests until
      you start and scale compute, while a warm standby already handles
      reduced traffic and only needs to scale up. Pilot light costs less
      and recovers more slowly. When a warm standby is fully scaled and
      serving full production load, it becomes hot standby.
Match the strategy to the recovery objectives you already defined.
      Avoid choosing one more stringent than the business requires,
      because standing capacity and cross-Region complexity carry
      ongoing cost. The following figure shows how a maximum acceptable
      RTO and a spending limit together narrow the field to the
      strategies that satisfy both. Where you want warm-standby recovery
      times closer to pilot-light cost, a purpose-built replication
      service can continuously protect data and orchestrate compute
      recovery on failover.
Choosing a disaster recovery strategy by RTO and cost
Replication alone does not make a workload recoverable. Continuous
      replication copies corruption and deletion to the recovery site as
      faithfully as it copies good data. Every strategy therefore needs
      point-in-time backups or versioning in addition to replication, so
      you can recover to a moment before the data was damaged.
Recovery is not complete when the recovery site takes over.
      Failback returns operation to the primary site, where data is the
      problem, and the recovery site now holds the current data.
      Resynchronize the primary site from it before switching back,
      sometimes by rebuilding the primary database as a replica of the
      recovery one. Some organizations avoid a rushed failback by
      promoting the recovery site to primary and rotating the roles on a
      schedule.
Implementation steps
Select a strategy that meets the
            objectives:
Compare your workload's RTO and RPO
            against the four strategies and choose the least costly one
            that satisfies both. Plot the target RTO against your cost
            ceiling, as shown in Figure 2, to see which strategies
            qualify. Avoid provisioning against objectives the business
            has not set. For the reasoning behind this choice, see
Business Continuity Plan (BCP)
.
Implement the pattern for your
            chosen strategy:
Build the recovery site
            according to the strategy you selected, from cross-site
            backups for backup and restore, to replicated data with
            dormant compute for pilot light, to a scaled-down live stack
            for warm standby, to live regional stacks for active-active.
            Use infrastructure as code so the recovery site is
            reproducible and consistent with the primary. For Amazon EC2-based workloads that suit a pilot-light cost profile
            with warm-standby speed, evaluate
AWS Elastic Disaster Recovery
.
Define the standing state of
            recovery-site resources:
Decide what runs in the
            recovery site during normal operation. Use
AWS CloudFormation
to provision infrastructure and
AWS CloudFormation StackSets
to deploy across accounts
            and Regions in one operation. Replicate data resources such
            as
Amazon RDS
databases or
Amazon DynamoDB
tables for pilot light, warm standby, and
            active-active so they are live in the recovery site. Use
AWS Backup
to schedule and monitor cross-Region backups.
Prepare the recovery site for
            failover:
Determine the actions needed to make
            the recovery site production-ready during an event. For
            pilot light and warm standby, deploy or scale the missing
            compute, and reserve capacity in advance with
Amazon EC2 capacity reservations
or
AWS Lambda provisioned concurrency
where needed. For all
            strategies, promote replica databases to primary as
            required. For backup and restore, restore data and rebuild
            infrastructure and code. Automate these actions so failover
            is repeatable.
Implement traffic
            redirection:
Decide how to reroute traffic to the
            recovery site, and prefer manually initiated failover with
            automated steps so a false alarm does not trigger an
            unnecessary, costly switch. For warm standby and multi-site
            active/active patterns, use
ARC Region Switch
to orchestrate the failover as a single
            operator-initiated operation with pre-flight checks and
            health validation. This is exactly the pattern of
            human-triggered but fully orchestrated failover. For complex
            multi-cell topologies requiring independent per-service
            routing decisions, use
Amazon Application Recovery Controller routing controls
. Use
            data plane operations during failover and avoid control
            plane dependencies, as described in
REL11-BP04 Rely on the data plane and not the control plane during recovery
.
Design and document
            failback:
Plan how you return to the primary site
            once the event is over, focusing on resynchronizing data
            from the recovery site to the primary. Note where managed
            replication restores the topology automatically, such as
Amazon DynamoDB global tables
or
Amazon Aurora Global Database managed planned failover
, and
            where you must rebuild manually. Capture the full failover
            and failback sequence in a playbook that the team reviews
            periodically.
